title: The Reading Crisis Is Neither New Nor Inevitable
author: Michele Caracappa
summary: Michele Caracappa responds to a viral Atlantic piece declaring 'the end of reading' by arguing that reading crises are neither new nor inevitable, and that doomsaying obscures the genuine agency school leaders possess to reverse the trend. She acknowledges the severity of the statistics—40% decline in pleasure reading over two decades, only 2% of adults reading to children on a given day—while insisting that how we frame a problem shapes how we solve it. The piece offers school leaders five concrete modes of action: modeling reading publicly, uniting communities around shared texts, investing in an expansive vision of literacy, organizing physical spaces to signal that reading matters, and going deep into texts with teacher teams before lesson planning begins.
points: The Atlantic's 'end of reading' framing, while statistically serious, obscures the agency school leaders have—the crisis framing in American education predates even 'A Nation at Risk.'
Modeling comes first: leaders who make their own reading life visible in signatures, office bookshelves, and PD sessions signal to communities that reading is a living practice, not a mandate.
One School, One Book initiatives and shared reading across faculty, students, and caregivers create community-level accountability and talking-about-texts culture.
Physical space is curriculum: how hallways, offices, and classrooms are organized either signals that literacy matters here or silently contradicts the stated commitment.
The deepest leadership lever is going into texts with teachers before lesson planning—asking 'what did you love or hate about this text?' before moving to instructional mechanics.
quotes: The reality is that the notion of a crisis of reading is neither new nor inevitable. As K-12 educators know, we've been teaching and learning amidst 'A Nation at Risk' for decades now, and the crisis framing has long preceded that.
On any given day, only two percent of American adults read to a child.

As a school leader, doing something about 'the end of reading' requires pushing back on the status quo. It requires cultivating a culture within your community that reinforces that reading matters and celebrates why it matters.

The way you organize the physical space within your school speaks volumes. Ask yourself, what would each space in my school community look like if it were impossible to miss that this is a school that is invested in reading and literacy?

Invest first in what I'd consider the most critical part of intellectual preparation—our own understanding of the texts, what's meaningful about them, and why they matter. Start your next planning meeting with teachers by asking, 'What did you love (or hate!) about this text?'

As Octavia Butler once wrote, 'there's no single answer that will solve all of our future problems. There's no magic bullet. Instead there are thousands of answers—at least. You can be one of them if you choose to be.'
